title: From Generalist to Specialist Representation
claim: Observations arise from latent states and actions, and tasks act as colliders across time steps, with each state component linking to multiple tasks.
layout: 2 panels, top-to-bottom, dashed blue zoom-in connecting overview graph to detail
description: A black-and-white causal graph with blue dashed highlights. The top panel shows a row of boxes, each holding a latent state and action (s1 a1, s2 a2, s3 a3, ..., st at), inside a large black dashed rounded rectangle. Upward arrows from each box lead to observations o1, o2, o3, ..., ot. A single arrow links s2 a2 to s3 a3, and the other boxes are disconnected from one another. Below the box, arrows from different time steps converge on task nodes g1, g2, ..., gM, which act as colliders. A blue dashed blob encloses st at and g1 and g2. A blue dashed arrow leads from the blob to a zoomed-in panel at the bottom. That panel shows state components s_{t,1} to s_{t,6} with crossing arrows through a dashed box labeled a_t into g1 and g2. The eye goes first to the top row of boxes and then follows the blue arrow down.
caption: An illustration of the generative process. Latent states st generate observations ot via nonlinear functions and interact with actions at under varying temporal connectivity, where consecutive steps may be arbitrarily disconnected. Tasks gi are defined as colliders across time steps, and different tasks can arbitrarily interleave with one another. The zoomed-in view (right) shows how different components of st connect to multiple tasks via the intermediate actions.
abstract: Given a generalist model, learning a task-relevant specialist representation is fundamental for downstream applications. Identifiability, the asymptotic guarantee of recovering the ground-truth representation, is critical because it sets the ultimate limit of any model, even with infinite data and computation. We study this problem in a completely nonparametric setting, without relying on interventions, parametric forms, or structural constraints. We first prove that the structure between time steps and tasks is identifiable in a fully unsupervised manner, even when sequences lack strict temporal dependence and may exhibit disconnections, and task assignments can follow arbitrarily complex and interleaving structures. We then prove that, within each time step, the task-relevant latent representation can be disentangled from the irrelevant part under a simple sparsity regularization, without any additional information or parametric constraints. Together, these results establish a hierarchical foundation: task structure is identifiable across time steps, and task-relevant latent representations are identifiable within each step. To our knowledge, each result provides a first general nonparametric identifiability guarantee, and together they mark a step toward provably moving from generalist to specialist models.
